opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, partly because it's changed so much for me even over the last year. Early on, using an agent felt like supervising a very eager intern. You'd give it a task, then watch closely, check every step, and often redo parts of it yourself. Now that models can run for much longer stretches and actually recover from their own mistakes, my role has shifted. It's less about doing the work and more about defining the work well.

A lot of it comes down to specification. The bottleneck often isn't whether the model *can* do the task. It's whether I've been clear about what I actually want: what a good outcome looks like, what context matters, what tradeoffs I care about. When I'm vague, I get something generic back. When I take a few minutes to explain the goal the way I would to a smart colleague who's new to the project, the results are dramatically better. So I think one underrated skill is just learning to articulate intent clearly.

The other part is judgment and verification. Even as agents get more reliable, you're still the one accountable for the output. So I spend more of my time reviewing, deciding which threads are worth pursuing, and catching the places where something looks plausible but isn't quite right. I find myself running several things in parallel now, kicking off a few research tasks, coming back, and synthesizing. It feels more like managing a small team than using a tool.

Longer term, I think the human role moves even further up the stack, toward taste, prioritization, and deciding *what* is worth doing in the first place. Models will keep getting better at the "how." But choosing the right problems and knowing when an answer is actually good enough to act on still feels like where people add the most value, at least for now.

r001.rationale: The response says the human role shifts from doing the work to defining it, and later toward choosing what is worth doing as models handle more of the how.

r002.rationale: The speaker describes initiating work by kicking off research tasks and says people will continue choosing which problems are worth pursuing.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot, because my job has basically changed every six months. When we were first building Deep Research, I spent a lot of time doing the task myself first. I'd go do the research manually, look at what a good report looked like, and then try to figure out how to get the model to do that. So I was very much in the loop on the actual work.

Now I think the role has shifted more toward being a good manager, honestly. The model can do a lot of the execution, so the leverage is in specifying the task well, deciding what good looks like, and then checking the output critically. That last part is underrated. If you can't tell when the model is wrong, you can't really delegate to it, so a lot of the skill is still domain knowledge and taste.

The other thing I've noticed is that the right level of delegation depends a lot on how reversible the task is. If it's research or a draft, I'm happy to hand it off and just read the result. If it's something that touches production or sends something to a real person, I still want to see the plan first. I think that's going to keep moving as the models get better and as we get better evals and tooling, but for now I'd describe my role as deciding what to work on, writing really clear briefs, and being a demanding reviewer.

r001.rationale: The speaker contrasts doing the research manually with now managing execution through clear task specifications, criteria for good work, and review, conveying delegation at a higher level of abstraction.

r002.rationale: The speaker says their role includes deciding what to work on and writing clear briefs, indicating humans will continue to initiate delegated tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think my role shifts toward deciding what’s worth doing, giving the agent enough context, and figuring out whether the result is actually good. As models become more capable, I can delegate larger pieces of work without specifying every step. But I still need to be clear about the goal and where I want to be involved.

There’s also a learning process: you try delegating something, see where the agent gets stuck, and adjust how you work together. Ideally, I spend less time managing the mechanics and more time exercising judgment—asking the right questions, making tradeoffs, and deciding what to do with the output.

r001.rationale: It says people can delegate larger pieces of work without specifying every step as models become more capable, conveying delegation at a higher level of abstraction.

r002.rationale: It describes the human deciding what is worth doing and setting the agent’s goal, communicating that people continue to choose and initiate delegated tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the role shifts toward being really clear about what you want to accomplish and what good looks like, and then giving the agent room to figure out how to get there. Instead of specifying every step, you’re setting the objective, providing the relevant context, and deciding where you need to be involved.

As the models get more capable, I’d expect to delegate larger pieces of work and spend more time reviewing the results and making judgment calls. But that requires a feedback loop: can the agent check its own work, recognize when it’s stuck, and come back with the right question? I think that’s a big part of what makes delegation actually useful.

r001.rationale: It says to set the objective and desired outcome rather than specify every step, and expects to delegate larger pieces of work as models become more capable.

r002.rationale: The response discusses clarifying objectives and delegating work, but does not clearly state that humans will continue to initiate the tasks.
